title: The study of the circumnuclear environment of accreting supermassive black holes with realistic X-ray spectral models
comment: 18 pages, 9 figures, the models are available: https://www.astro.unige.ch/reflex/xspec-models
summary: X-ray spectral modeling is a powerful tool for studying the immediate environment of accreting objects, including supermassive black holes. Several models, either phenomenological or physically driven, have been developed over the past decade to study X-ray spectra, delivering important insights into the properties of circumnuclear material of active galactic nuclei (AGN). Despite the fact that these models are able to reproduce the data well, they often lack realistic geometries, and most of them consist of simplified configurations such as a slab or a torus. We use the ray-tracing code \textsc{RefleX} to generate new spectral models that cover a wide energy range in the X-ray band, adopting a realistic configuration for the surrounding material. We introduce two new table models that are publicly available: 1) the RXToPo model, which features an X-ray source along with a dusty torus and a polar hollow cone; 2) the RXagn1 model, which includes, besides the torus and polar cone, also the accretion disk and the broad line region. Both models were applied to the X-ray spectrum of NGC 424, demonstrating their potential to study sources whose X-ray emission is dominated by reprocessed radiation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces two new X-ray spectral models (RXToPo and RXagn1) that use realistic geometries (dusty torus, polar cone, accretion disk, broad line region) generated with the ray-tracing code RefleX, applied to the AGN NGC 424 to study reprocessed X-ray emission.
AI.motivation: Existing X-ray spectral models for AGN often rely on oversimplified geometries (e.g., slab or torus) that lack realistic configurations, limiting their ability to accurately describe the circumnuclear environment of accreting supermassive black holes.
AI.method: The authors use the ray-tracing code RefleX to generate spectral models with realistic geometries. They introduce two table models: RXToPo (X-ray source + dusty torus + polar hollow cone) and RXagn1 (torus, polar cone, accretion disk, and broad line region). These models are applied to the X-ray spectrum of NGC 424.
AI.result: Both RXToPo and RXagn1 successfully reproduced the X-ray spectrum of NGC 424, demonstrating their capability to study sources where X-ray emission is dominated by reprocessed radiation.
AI.conclusion: The new models offer more realistic geometries for X-ray spectral fitting of AGN, enabling better characterization of reprocessed emission and the circumnuclear material around supermassive black holes.

title: X-ray spectroscopy mass constraints on V1674 Her: the fastest nova does not have a near-Chandrasekhar white dwarf
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: V1674 Her (Nova Her 2021) is the fastest classical nova ever recorded, with an optical decline time of $t_2 \sim 1$ day, typically interpreted as evidence for a white dwarf mass close to the Chandrasekhar limit. We present a broadband X-ray study of V1674 Her combining contemporaneous XMM-Newton and NuSTAR observations in quiescence to directly constrain the white dwarf mass and magnetic field strength. The hard X-ray emission is modeled using a physically motivated post-shock accretion column model that accounts for the temperature gradient in the flow and reflection from the white dwarf surface. Under the assumption that the accretion disk is truncated at the co-rotation radius, we obtain a white dwarf mass of $M = 1.09^{+0.07}_{-0.06}\,M_\odot$. An independent constraint derived from timing analysis of the X-ray power spectrum yields a consistent value of $M = 1.12 \pm 0.06\,M_\odot$. These values are significantly lower than those inferred from empirical decline-time relations, suggesting that such relations may overestimate white dwarf masses in extreme fast novae. From the inferred accretion rate and magnetospheric radius, we estimate a surface magnetic field strength of $B = 21.3^{+6.6}_{-5.7}\,(\mathrm{stat})^{+12.9}_{-8.1}\,(\mathrm{sys})\,\mathrm{MG}$, placing V1674 Her at the high end of the magnetic field distribution for intermediate polars. Our results demonstrate that even the fastest novae do not necessarily host near-Chandrasekhar white dwarfs, highlighting the importance of direct X-ray constraints and suggesting that additional parameters beyond white dwarf mass play a key role in setting nova timescales.

AI.tldr: V1674 Her, the fastest classical nova (t₂~1 day), was studied via XMM-Newton and NuSTAR X-ray observations. Using post-shock accretion column modeling and timing analysis, the white dwarf mass is constrained to ~1.09-1.12 M☉, significantly lower than Chandrasekhar-limit estimates from empirical decline-time relations. The surface magnetic field is ~21 MG, placing it at the high end for intermediate polars. This suggests nova timescales depend on additional parameters beyond WD mass.
AI.motivation: V1674 Her is the fastest classical nova ever observed (t₂~1 day), which implies a white dwarf mass near the Chandrasekhar limit based on standard empirical decline-time relations. The authors aim to directly constrain the white dwarf mass and magnetic field strength using broadband X-ray observations to test whether extreme speed necessarily implies near-Chandrasekhar mass.
AI.method: Contemporaneous XMM-Newton and NuSTAR observations were used. Hard X-ray emission was modeled with a physically motivated post-shock accretion column model that includes temperature gradients and reflection from the WD surface. The white dwarf mass was derived under the assumption that the accretion disk truncates at the co-rotation radius. An independent constraint came from X-ray timing analysis (power spectrum). The magnetic field was estimated from accretion rate and magnetospheric radius.
AI.result: White dwarf mass from accretion column modeling: M = 1.09⁺⁰·⁰⁷₋₀·₀₆ M☉. From timing analysis: M = 1.12 ± 0.06 M☉. Both are significantly lower than Chandrasekhar-mass predictions from decline-time relations. Surface magnetic field: B = 21.3⁺⁶·⁶₋₅·₇ (stat)⁺¹²·⁹₋₈·₁ (sys) MG.
AI.conclusion: Even the fastest classical novae do not necessarily host near-Chandrasekhar white dwarfs. Empirical decline-time relations may overestimate WD masses in extreme fast novae. Additional parameters beyond WD mass (e.g., magnetic field, accretion rate) play a key role in setting nova timescales. Direct X-ray constraints are essential for accurate mass measurements.

title: Nuclear Constraints on $^{12}$C$(α,γ)^{16}$O and Their Impact on Black-Hole Mass Predictions
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures
summary:
Gravitational-wave observations have renewed interest in the black-hole mass gap and in the maximum mass of first-generation black holes below its lower edge. The \(^{12}{\rm C}(α,γ)^{16}{\rm O}\) reaction plays a central role in this problem because it determines the carbon-to-oxygen ratio after core-helium burning and thereby affects the later evolution of massive stars toward pulsational pair instability and pair-instability supernovae.
  Recent attempts to constrain \(S(300~{\rm keV})\) from gravitational-wave population inferences face important limitations, because the lower edge of the black-hole mass gap is not directly measured. It is inferred model dependently from assumptions about stellar evolution, metallicity, mass loss, rotation, binary evolution, hierarchical mergers, selection effects, priors, and the adopted population model. Therefore, values of \(S(300~{\rm keV})\) inferred from black-hole populations must remain consistent with independent nuclear-physics constraints.
  In this work we reanalyze the low-energy \(^{12}{\rm C}(α,γ)^{16}{\rm O}\) \(S\) factor using updated information on the subthreshold \(1^{-}\) and \(2^{+}\) ANCs and on the ground-state ANC of \(^{16}{\rm O}\), together with direct capture data. These constraints favor a lower \(S(300~{\rm keV})\) than the older central evaluation and disfavor very large values required by some black-hole-population interpretations. Using the resulting ANC-constrained \(S(300~{\rm keV})\) range and the transformed relation between this quantity and the lower edge of the pair-instability mass gap, we estimate \[ \frac{M_{\rm BH}}{M_\odot}\simeq 61\text{--}75 . \] Thus, the present nuclear-physics constraints favor a relatively high lower edge of the first-generation black-hole mass gap.

AI.tldr: Nuclear constraints on the ¹²C(α,γ)¹⁶O reaction favor a lower S(300 keV) value, which pushes the lower edge of the first-generation black-hole mass gap to M_BH/M_⊙ ≈ 61–75, disfavoring very large S factors inferred from some gravitational-wave population models.
AI.motivation: To resolve tensions between gravitational-wave population inferences of the black-hole mass gap lower edge and independent nuclear-physics constraints, by reanalyzing the ¹²C(α,γ)¹⁶O S factor which governs the C/O ratio after core-helium burning and thus affects stellar evolution toward pair-instability supernovae.
AI.method: Reanalysis of the low-energy ¹²C(α,γ)¹⁶O S factor using updated asymptotic normalization coefficients (ANCs) for subthreshold 1⁻ and 2⁺ states and the ground-state ANC of ¹⁶O, combined with direct capture data.
AI.result: The ANC-constrained S(300 keV) is lower than older central evaluations and disfavors very large values required by some BH-population interpretations. The derived lower edge of the first-generation BH mass gap is M_BH/M_⊙ ≈ 61–75.
AI.conclusion: Nuclear-physics constraints favor a relatively high lower edge of the first-generation black-hole mass gap, and S(300 keV) values inferred from BH populations must remain consistent with independent nuclear-physics constraints.

title: Anisotropic Thermal Conduction as a Driver of Jet Collimation and Magnetic Field Amplification on Cold Fronts
summary: Galaxy clusters contain a hot, diffuse, and weakly magnetized plasma known as the intracluster medium (ICM). In this environment, how thermal conduction influences plasma dynamics and the conditions under which it operates efficiently remain open questions in cluster physics. Systems in which active galactic nuclei (AGN) jets interact with cold fronts produced by cluster mergers provide a unique setting to examine the interplay between conduction, jet dynamics, and ordered magnetic fields. To interpret the detailed structures revealed by recent observations, it is therefore important, as a first theoretical step, to quantify how thermal conduction modifies AGN jet morphology and the surrounding magnetic-field configuration. We perform two-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of an AGN jet in an ICM environment, incorporating anisotropic thermal conduction with varying efficiency. The simulations show that thermal conduction transports heat from the jet head backward along magnetic field lines into the inner cocoon. This process increases the inner cocoon pressure, enhancing jet collimation by a factor of $\sim 4$ compared to models without conduction. This stronger collimation stretches the magnetic fields along the cold-front surface, resulting in a maximum field strength up to a factor of $\sim 1.5$ larger. Jet collimation increases as the conduction efficiency increases, which is interpreted as a conductive collimation mechanism. These results suggest that anisotropic thermal conduction can operate effectively on jet scales in galaxy clusters, and that accounting for conduction may be important when interpreting jet morphology and magnetic field structure in merging cluster environments.

AI.tldr: This study uses 2D MHD simulations to show that anisotropic thermal conduction in the intracluster medium transports heat from AGN jet heads backward along magnetic field lines, increasing inner cocoon pressure and enhancing jet collimation by ~4x and magnetic field strength by ~1.5x, revealing a conductive collimation mechanism important for interpreting jet morphology in merging clusters.
AI.motivation: To understand how thermal conduction influences plasma dynamics in the ICM, particularly in systems where AGN jets interact with cold fronts from cluster mergers, and to provide a theoretical foundation for interpreting recent high-resolution observations of jet morphology and magnetic field structures.
AI.method: Two-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of an AGN jet in an ICM environment, incorporating anisotropic thermal conduction with varying efficiency.
AI.result: Thermal conduction transports heat from the jet head backward along field lines into the inner cocoon, increasing inner cocoon pressure and enhancing jet collimation by ~4x compared to models without conduction. Maximum magnetic field strength increases by ~1.5x. Jet collimation increases with conduction efficiency, indicating a conductive collimation mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Anisotropic thermal conduction can operate effectively on jet scales in galaxy clusters, and accounting for conduction is important when interpreting jet morphology and magnetic field structure in merging cluster environments.

title: Complex organic molecules and cosmic ray ionisation rate towards the massive protostar Cepheus A HW2
comment: Submitted to A&A, comments are welcome. 20 pages, 18 figures
summary: Cosmic rays (CRs) are important drivers for molecular chemistry in star-forming regions, and laboratory experiments have shown that CRs can stimulate the release of complex organic molecules (COMs) such as methanol. Observationally, this has primarily been tested in cold, low-mass cores, so studying how CRs affect COM formation in a high-mass star-forming environment is of great interest. We performed a high-sensitivity wide-band spectral line survey with the Onsala 20 m telescope towards the high-mass protostar Cepheus A HW2, which is known to host an ionised jet. Consistent with previous studies, two primary velocity components ($-11$ km s$^{-1}$ and $-5$ km s$^{-1}$) were identified. Column densities and relative abundances of the detected ions and COMs were estimated from rotational diagrams, single transitions and RADEX grid searches (CH$_3$OH: $1.6\times10^{-9}$, CH$_3$CN: $5.9\times10^{-11}$, t-HCOOH: $7.9\times10^{-11}$, H$_2$CCO: $1.7\times10^{-11}$, CH$_3$CHO: $1.9\times10^{-11}$, CH$_3$OCHO: $7.6\times10^{-10}$ at $-11$ km s$^{-1}$). Deuterium fractions were also estimated (in range $0.002-0.3$ at $-11$ km s$^{-1}$), and the volume density of molecular hydrogen ($2.6\times10^5$ cm$^{-3}$ at $-11$ km s$^{-1}$) was constrained from the RADEX grid searches. Electron fractions and CR ionisation rates (CRIR, $6.8\times10^{-17}$ s$^{-1}$ at $-11$ km s$^{-1}$, $\leq9.2\times10^{-19}$ s$^{-1}$ at $-5$ km s$^{-1}$) were estimated through analytic chemistry using different ions as probes. The gas-grain chemical code Nautilus reproduced the observed abundances of CH$_3$OH, CH$_3$CN, HCO$^+$, N$_2$H$^+$ at the observed density, temperature and CRIR within the uncertainty of the model. The results indicate that the CR ionisation rate of the kinematic component associated with most of the COMs' emission in the region is locally enhanced.

AI.tldr: This study investigates cosmic ray ionization rates and complex organic molecule chemistry in the high-mass protostar Cepheus A HW2 using spectral line survey data, finding locally enhanced CR ionization rates and successfully reproducing observed abundances with chemical modeling.
AI.motivation: To understand how cosmic rays influence complex organic molecule (COM) formation in high-mass star-forming environments, as previous studies focused primarily on cold, low-mass cores.
AI.method: High-sensitivity wide-band spectral line survey with Onsala 20 m telescope toward Cepheus A HW2; column density estimation via rotational diagrams, single transitions, and RADEX grid searches; electron fractions and CR ionization rates derived through analytic chemistry using ions as probes; gas-grain chemical code Nautilus for abundance reproduction.
AI.result: Detected two velocity components (-11 and -5 km/s); derived column densities for COMs (e.g., CH₃OH: 1.6×10⁻⁹, CH₃OCHO: 7.6×10⁻¹⁰ at -11 km/s); deuterium fractions 0.002-0.3; CR ionization rates of 6.8×10⁻¹⁷ s⁻¹ (at -11 km/s) and ≤9.2×10⁻¹⁹ s⁻¹ (at -5 km/s); Nautilus model reproduced observed abundances within uncertainties.
AI.conclusion: The CR ionization rate of the kinematic component associated with most COM emission is locally enhanced in this high-mass star-forming region.

title: Resonant Inverse Compton Scattering and Hard X-ray Emission in Magnetar Magnetospheres
comment: 20 pages, 13 figures, submitted to ApJ
summary: Magnetars are a subclass of neutron stars with ultra-strong surface magnetic fields. Some magnetars exhibit persistent hard X-ray emission, characterized by power-law tails with photon indices around 1--1.5, extending from ${\sim}$10 keV to several hundred keV. The leading explanation for this hard X-ray component is resonant Compton scattering, in which the thermal seed photons are upscattered by relativistic electron-positron pairs flowing along magnetic field lines in the magnetosphere. In this work, we adopt the pair outflow framework of the magnetar magnetosphere and calculate the resonant Compton scattering opacity, as well as the spectrum and polarization of the upscattered emission. We find that resonant cooling can substantially modify the magnetospheric plasma density and impose strong optical depth constraints on the hard X-ray emission regions. Under the viewing geometry inferred from IXPE, an equatorial twist near the stellar surface provides a viable configuration for the NuSTAR hard X-ray spectrum of 4U 0142+61, while a polar-twist geometry is disfavored. Joint spectral, timing, and polarimetric modeling will be essential for distinguishing between the magnetospheric scattering geometries and understanding the physical properties of the pair plasma.

AI.tldr: This paper models resonant Compton scattering in magnetar magnetospheres, showing that resonant cooling affects plasma density and optical depth, and that an equatorial twist geometry near the stellar surface best explains NuSTAR hard X-ray spectrum of 4U 0142+61, while polar-twist is disfavored.
AI.motivation: To understand the origin of persistent hard X-ray emission (power-law tails from ~10 keV to hundreds of keV) observed in some magnetars, which is hypothesized to arise from resonant Compton scattering of thermal seed photons by relativistic electron-positron pairs in the magnetosphere.
AI.method: The authors adopt a pair outflow framework of the magnetar magnetosphere, calculate the resonant Compton scattering opacity, and compute the spectrum and polarization of the upscattered emission under different magnetic twist geometries (equatorial vs. polar).
AI.result: Resonant cooling substantially modifies the magnetospheric plasma density and imposes strong optical depth constraints on hard X-ray emission regions. An equatorial twist near the stellar surface reproduces the NuSTAR hard X-ray spectrum of 4U 0142+61 under IXPE-inferred viewing geometry, whereas a polar-twist geometry is disfavored.
AI.conclusion: Joint spectral, timing, and polarimetric modeling is essential to distinguish between magnetospheric scattering geometries and to understand the physical properties of the pair plasma.

title: Diffuse gamma-ray emissions around the stellar cluster Berkeley 59
summary: We report a detailed analysis on the young stellar cluster Berkeley 59 using Fermi-LAT. Using up-to-date source catalog and background models, we found significant extended GeV emission around Berkeley 59, which can be modeled by a radial disk of 1.02 degree radius with a significance of the extension of 10.6 sigma. We investigated the molecular, neutral and ionized gas content and the hadronic origin. The gamma-ray spectrum of Berkeley 59 has a photon index of 2.88. The derived gas mass from H2 and HII around Berkeley 59 is about 289 solar mass. We derived the relationship between cosmic ray acceleration efficiency and diffusion coefficient. Our results suggest that the extended gamma-ray emission originates from cosmic rays accelerated by cluster winds interacting with surrounding gas.

AI.tldr: Using Fermi-LAT data, the study detects significant extended GeV emission around the young stellar cluster Berkeley 59 (1.02° radius, 10.6σ significance), modeled with a photon index of 2.88. The emission likely originates from cosmic rays accelerated by cluster winds interacting with ambient gas, with a derived gas mass of ~289 M☉ from H2 and HII regions.
AI.motivation: To investigate the origin of extended gamma-ray emission around the young stellar cluster Berkeley 59, specifically testing whether cosmic rays accelerated by cluster winds interacting with surrounding gas can explain the observed emission.
AI.method: Fermi-LAT data analysis using up-to-date source catalog and background models; spatial modeling with a radial disk of 1.02° radius; investigation of molecular, neutral, and ionized gas content; hadronic origin analysis; derivation of cosmic ray acceleration efficiency and diffusion coefficient relationship.
AI.result: Significant extended GeV emission detected around Berkeley 59 (10.6σ extension significance, 1.02° radius disk); gamma-ray spectrum photon index of 2.88; derived gas mass from H2 and HII regions ~289 M☉.
AI.conclusion: The extended gamma-ray emission originates from cosmic rays accelerated by cluster winds interacting with surrounding gas.

title: KM3-230213A and potential astrophysical sources
comment: Contribution to the 2026 Very High Energy Phenomena in the Universe session of the 60th Rencontres de Moriond
summary: The recent detection of the ultra-high energy neutrino KM3-230213A by KM3NeT/ARCA marks the first observation of an astrophysical neutrino with energy above 100 PeV, opening a new window to the ultra-high energy Universe. In this contribution, the current global ultra-high energy neutrino landscape in light of this event is reviewed, including tension of this observation with existing limits set by the IceCube and the Pierre Auger Observatories. Different scenarios are discussed to explain its origin. Recent efforts to constrain features of potential source populations using the inferred diffuse ultra-high energy neutrino flux are also presented.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews the first ultra-high energy neutrino (>100 PeV) detected by KM3NeT/ARCA (KM3-230213A), examines its tension with IceCube and Pierre Auger limits, and discusses possible astrophysical origins and constraints on source populations from the inferred diffuse flux.
AI.motivation: The detection of KM3-230213A by KM3NeT/ARCA, the first neutrino above 100 PeV, opens a new observational window to the ultra-high energy Universe. This event challenges existing flux limits, necessitating a re-evaluation of the current UHE neutrino landscape and its origins.
AI.method: The study reviews the global UHE neutrino landscape in light of KM3-230213A, compares it with existing limits from IceCube and Pierre Auger, discusses potential astrophysical origin scenarios, and presents constraints on source population features derived from the inferred diffuse UHE neutrino flux.
AI.result: KM3-230213A is the first astrophysical neutrino detected above 100 PeV, and its observation is in tension with existing limits from IceCube and Pierre Auger. Constraints on source population characteristics are derived from the diffuse UHE neutrino flux inferred from this event.
AI.conclusion: KM3-230213A heralds a new era in UHE neutrino astronomy, but its high flux relative to previous limits indicates either a non-steady source population or a need to revise current flux models. Further multi-messenger observations are required to resolve the tension and identify the origin.

title: Advance warning of $γ$-ray blazar flares from \textit{Fermi}-LAT light curves: a strictly causal machine-learning backtest
summary: Long-term \textit{Fermi}-LAT monitoring makes it possible to ask whether a blazar light curve shows signs of an upcoming flare before the flare becomes obvious in the $γ$-ray emission. We present a strictly causal machine-learning framework for forecasting $γ$-ray blazar flares from 3-d binned LAT light curves. Flare intervals are identified with Bayesian Blocks, and each light curve is sampled with 365-d trailing windows from which 42 variability features are measured. We train separate WATCH and TRIGGER models: WATCH predicts whether flare activity will appear within the next 90 d, while TRIGGER predicts whether a new flare onset will occur within the next 45 d. To avoid temporal leakage, all scaling, calibration, threshold selection, and validation use only the pre-cutoff data before MJD 60000. We apply the method to the FSRQ 4FGL\,J1048.4$+$7143, using 13 bright blazars as auxiliary training sources. Among logistic regression, polynomial logistic regression, and random forest classifiers, polynomial logistic regression gives the strongest held-out WATCH performance, with ROC AUC $=0.891$, average precision $=0.396$, and a block-permutation probability $p_{\rm perm}=0.006$. At the selected WATCH threshold, it recovers 18 of the 21 positive windows in the held-out WATCH set, corresponding to a recall of 0.86. The same model also gives the best held-out TRIGGER ranking, with TRIGGER AUC $=0.770$ and TRIGGER AP $=0.123$, although no reliable pre-onset TRIGGER alert is obtained. The WATCH state appears before both held-out flare episodes, with final alerts 4.5 and 2.5 d before onset. The corresponding broader WATCH-active periods begin 88.5 and 72.5 d before flare onset. These results suggest that long-term {\fermi} light curves contain useful predictive information about the build-up to blazar flares.

AI.tldr: A strictly causal machine-learning framework forecasts γ-ray blazar flares from 3-d binned Fermi-LAT light curves using WATCH (flare activity within 90d) and TRIGGER (flare onset within 45d) models. Polynomial logistic regression yields best held-out WATCH performance (ROC AUC=0.891) and can provide alerts days to weeks before flare onset.
AI.motivation: To determine whether long-term Fermi-LAT monitoring of blazar light curves contains predictive signals that can forecast upcoming γ-ray flares before they become obvious, enabling earlier astronomical alerts.
AI.method: Bayesian Blocks identify flare intervals; 42 variability features are extracted from 365-d trailing windows. Separate WATCH (90-d flare activity) and TRIGGER (45-d flare onset) classifiers are trained (logistic regression, polynomial logistic regression, random forest) with strict causal separation (pre-cutoff data before MJD 60000) to avoid temporal leakage. Applied to FSRQ 4FGL J1048.4+7143 with 13 bright blazars as auxiliary training sources.
AI.result: Polynomial logistic regression achieves best held-out WATCH performance: ROC AUC=0.891, average precision=0.396, p_perm=0.006, recall=0.86 (18/21 positive windows). Same model gives TRIGGER AUC=0.770, AP=0.123 (no reliable pre-onset alert). WATCH alerts occurred 4.5 and 2.5 d before flare onset; WATCH-active periods began 88.5 and 72.5 d before onset.
AI.conclusion: Long-term Fermi-LAT light curves contain useful predictive information about the build-up to blazar flares, enabling forecasts days to weeks in advance with a strictly causal machine-learning framework.

title: Radial redistribution of stellar orbits in FIRE simulations of Milky-Way-mass galaxies
comment: 23 pages, submitted to The Open Journal of Astrophysics
summary: A central question in galactic dynamics and galactic archeology is: how much do the orbits of stars redistribute (migrate) after birth? We use the FIRE-2 cosmological zoom-in simulations of 11 Milky Way-mass galaxies to quantify the change in the orbital specific angular momentum, j_phi, orbital radius, R_orbit, and azimuthal velocity, v_phi, of stars from birth to today. We examine the dependences on stellar age, present-day R_orbit, and birth R_orbit, characterizing both the median (net) change, Delta R_orbit, and its scatter, sigma(Delta R_orbit). We comprehensively compare five ways of measuring orbital radius; we find generally consistent trends, but only when measuring radius today and radial redistribution self-consistently. Stars selected by their birth R_orbit typically decreased in R_orbit, j_phi, and v_phi since birth. The trend for stars at a given R_orbit today depends on age: those younger than ~5 Gyr generally decreased in R_orbit, j_phi, and v_phi since birth, while those older generally increased in R_orbit, j_phi, and v_phi since birth. sigma(Delta R_orbit), a standard metric of radial redistribution, increases with stellar age only up to ~ 3 Gyr; it saturates at sigma(Delta R_orbit) ~2 kpc for older stars. This saturation contradicts a common expectation of a monotonic increase with age. Our results broadly agree with recent observational inferences of Delta R_orbit and sigma(Delta R_orbit) in the Milky Way. Across our FIRE-2 sample, the timing of disk formation does not correlate with sigma(Delta R_orbit), but it correlates with (net) Delta R_orbit.

AI.tldr: Using FIRE-2 simulations of 11 Milky Way-mass galaxies, this paper studies how stars' orbital properties (angular momentum, radius, azimuthal velocity) change from birth to present day, finding that radial migration scatter saturates at ~2 kpc after 3 Gyr, contradicting expectations of monotonic increase with age.
AI.motivation: To understand how much stars redistribute orbitally after birth, a central question for galactic dynamics and archeology, by quantifying changes in orbital specific angular momentum, radius, and azimuthal velocity across stellar ages and radii.
AI.method: Analysis of FIRE-2 cosmological zoom-in simulations of 11 Milky Way-mass galaxies, comparing five different ways of measuring orbital radius, examining dependences on stellar age, present-day R_orbit, and birth R_orbit, and characterizing median changes and scatter.
AI.result: Stars selected by birth radius typically decreased in R_orbit, j_phi, and v_phi. Present-day radius trends depend on age: younger than ~5 Gyr decreased, older increased. The scatter sigma(Delta R_orbit) saturates at ~2 kpc for stars older than 3 Gyr, not increasing monotonically with age. Disk formation timing correlates with net Delta R_orbit but not with sigma(Delta R_orbit).
AI.conclusion: Radial migration scatter saturates at ~2 kpc after ~3 Gyr, contradicting the common expectation of monotonic increase with age. Results broadly agree with recent Milky Way observational inferences.

title: Young Massive Star Clusters as TeV Emitters: Constraints from H.E.S.S. and LHAASO
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A 07 May 2026
summary: Young massive star clusters (YMSCs) have been proposed as excellent candidates for the main sources of Galactic cosmic rays (CRs) up to the PeV range. The detection and study of gamma rays in the very-high-energy (E>100GeV) range has brought arguments in favour of this hypothesis. Current instruments have detected only a few YMSCs. Future observatories are expected to increase this number, providing a larger sample improving our ability to constrain the role of YMSCs in the origin of CRs. We study the population of TeV YMSCs detected and their properties, confronting simulations of the YMSC population to the observed sample, to address the fundamental questions concerning the spectrum of accelerated particles, the efficiency of CR production, and the fraction of the wind luminosity converted into turbulent magnetic fields. Using Monte Carlo methods, we simulate the Galactic population of YMSCs in the gamma-ray domain and confront our simulations to the catalogue of sources of the systematic survey of the Galactic plane performed by H.E.S.S. (HGPS) and the First LHAASO Catalogue of Gamma-Ray Sources. We systematically explore the parameter space of our model, including the slope of accelerated particles $α$, the CR efficiency $η_{\rm CR}$, the fraction of the wind luminosity converted into turbulent magnetic field $η_{\rm b}$, and the diffusion regime. We found 5 possible sets of parameters for which >75% of realisations agree with the combined data from the HGPS and LHAASO 1st catalogue. Certain regions of the parameter space are strongly disfavoured, such as Bohm diffusion. Our model successfully reproduces the YMSC population observed in both catalogues. With future systematic surveys, e.g. the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO), this approach will help break degeneracies and improve our understanding of particle acceleration at YMSC shocks in the Galaxy.

AI.tldr: This study uses Monte Carlo simulations of Galactic YMSC populations to model TeV gamma-ray emission, comparing against H.E.S.S. and LHAASO catalogs to constrain particle acceleration slope, CR efficiency, and magnetic turbulence fraction, finding 5 viable parameter sets with Bohm diffusion disfavored.
AI.motivation: YMSCs are proposed as major sources of Galactic CRs up to PeV energies, but only a few have been detected. A larger observed sample is needed to constrain their role in CR origin.
AI.method: Monte Carlo simulations of the Galactic YMSC population in gamma rays, compared against HGPS and First LHAASO Catalogue, systematically exploring parameters including particle slope α, CR efficiency η_CR, magnetic turbulence fraction η_b, and diffusion regime.
AI.result: 5 parameter sets yield >75% agreement with combined HGPS+LHAASO data; Bohm diffusion is strongly disfavored.
AI.conclusion: The model successfully reproduces observed YMSC populations; future surveys like CTAO will help break degeneracies and improve understanding of particle acceleration at YMSC shocks.

title: The galaxy ultraviolet luminosity function from $z=7$ to $15$ in the COLIBRE simulations
comment: 28 pages, 16 figures; submitted to MNRAS
summary: JWST has enabled the detection of galaxies in the earliest stages of cosmic history. We compare the ultraviolet luminosity functions (UVLFs) at redshifts $z=7-15$ predicted by the new cosmological hydrodynamics simulations, COLIBRE with observations, including those from JWST. The UV luminosities of COLIBRE galaxies are derived using the radiative transfer code SKIRT, which tracks stellar emission and its processing through the multi-phase interstellar medium and dust distribution predicted by COLIBRE. We find that although COLIBRE is consistent with the observed evolution of the stellar mass function up to $z=12$, its dust-attenuated UVLFs fall systematically below the observations at the bright end: at the number density of $10^{-6}\,\mathrm{Mpc^{-3}\,mag^{-1}}$, the brightest galaxies are underluminous by $\approx 1\,\rm mag$ at $z=7$, increasing to $\approx 2.5\,\rm mag$ at $z=15$. Accounting for observational uncertainties brings the COLIBRE UVLFs closer to the observational data, but does not fully resolve the discrepancy. Ignoring dust attenuation allows COLIBRE to produce sufficiently bright galaxies at $7\lesssim z \lesssim 12$, while at $z=15$, COLIBRE still underpredicts the luminosities of the brightest galaxies, indicating the need for additional physical mechanisms to boost the UV luminosities at the earliest cosmic epochs, such as a ''top-heavy'' stellar initial mass function. We fit the COLIBRE UVLFs with Schechter functions and calculate the evolution of the best-fit parameters. We find that the galaxy number density decreases, the characteristic luminosity becomes fainter and the faint-end slope becomes steeper towards higher redshifts. The UV luminosity density decreases by a factor of $\approx 300$ from $z = 7$ to $z = 15$.

AI.tldr: The COLIBRE cosmological simulations, when compared to JWST observations, produce galaxies that are systematically underluminous in the UV at high redshifts (z=7-15). Even when accounting for observational uncertainties, the brightest simulated galaxies are 1-2.5 magnitudes fainter than observed. While removing dust attenuation resolves the discrepancy at z=7-12, it fails at z=15, suggesting additional physics (e.g., top-heavy IMF) is needed. The UV luminosity density drops by ~300× from z=7 to z=15.
AI.motivation: To test whether state-of-the-art cosmological hydrodynamics simulations (COLIBRE) can reproduce the UV luminosity functions of high-redshift galaxies (z=7-15) observed by JWST, and to identify any physical mechanisms missing from current simulations.
AI.method: The authors compare COLIBRE simulation UVLFs (processed through the SKIRT radiative transfer code for dust attenuation) against JWST observations at z=7-15. They apply Schechter function fitting, account for observational uncertainties, and test scenarios with and without dust attenuation.
AI.result: COLIBRE UVLFs are systematically underluminous at the bright end by ~1 mag at z=7 to ~2.5 mag at z=15. Removing dust fixes the discrepancy at z=7-12 but not at z=15. The UV luminosity density decreases by ~300× from z=7 to z=15.
AI.conclusion: Current simulations lack mechanisms to produce the brightest galaxies at the earliest epochs (z=15). A top-heavy IMF or other exotic physics may be required, while at lower redshifts (z=7-12), dust attenuation modeling is the dominant source of discrepancy.

title: Detection of persistent helium absorption in the 91bg-like type Ia Supernova 2022an
comment: Submitted to the AAS journal. Comments are welcome
summary: We present optical and near-infrared observations of the fast-declining Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) 2022an. The photometric and spectroscopic properties identify it as a standard 91bg-like event; however, our data reveal a relatively narrow absorption feature with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 75 angstroms near $1.037\,μ$m in the rest frame of the observed spectra that persists from around 30 days to nearly 90 days after maximum light. We attribute this feature to He I $1.083\,μ$m line with a blueshifted velocity of $1.3\times10^{4}$ km s$^{-1}$ and a FWHM of $2.1\times10^{3}$ km s$^{-1}$, supported by the detection of multiple optical He I transitions in earlier epochs at a higher velocity around $1.5\times10^{4}$ km s$^{-1}$. The high velocity of the helium could not be explained by helium external to the progenitor at the explosion, such as the stripped surface helium from a companion star. The properties of the helium absorption in SN 2022an spectra instead point to unburnt material in the outer ejecta, thus providing the most compelling evidence to date for helium-bearing ejecta in a 91bg-like SN Ia. Such helium has been predicted for sub-Chandrasekhar-mass double-detonation explosions involving a surface helium shell. No theoretical calculations of modern helium-shell double detonation have been performed at epochs similar to those observed for SN 2022an to study the effect of helium on their spectra, revealing a gap between observations and theoretical calculations in understanding the manifestation of helium in SNe Ia. Nevertheless, the discovery of persistent helium absorption in SN 2022an demonstrates the diagnostic power of NIR spectroscopy for understanding thermonuclear supernova explosions by probing the abundance and structure of their ejecta.

AI.tldr: SN 2022an, a 91bg-like Type Ia supernova, shows persistent He I absorption in NIR spectra (30–90 days post-maximum), with blueshifted velocity ~1.3×10⁴ km/s, indicating helium in the outer ejecta rather than stripped from a companion. This supports a sub-Chandrasekhar double-detonation origin and highlights NIR spectroscopy as a diagnostic tool, though theoretical models at these late epochs are lacking.
AI.motivation: To investigate the origin of helium absorption in a fast-declining 91bg-like SN Ia and to test whether such helium comes from external stripped material or from intrinsic unburnt ejecta, thereby distinguishing between progenitor scenarios (e.g., double-detonation vs. single degenerate).
AI.method: Optical and near-infrared photometry and spectroscopy of SN 2022an; measurement of absorption feature FWHM and blueshift velocity; comparison with optical He I transitions and existing theoretical models.
AI.result: Detection of persistent He I 1.083 μm absorption (FWHM 75 Å, blueshift ~1.3×10⁴ km/s) from ~30 to 90 days post-maximum, with optical He I lines at higher velocity (~1.5×10⁴ km/s) at earlier epochs. The high velocity rules out external stripped helium, pointing instead to unburnt helium in the outer ejecta.
AI.conclusion: SN 2022an provides the strongest evidence for helium-bearing ejecta in a 91bg-like SN Ia, consistent with a sub-Chandrasekhar double-detonation model with a surface helium shell. However, a gap exists between observations and theoretical calculations for these late epochs, and NIR spectroscopy is a powerful tool for probing ejecta composition and structure.

title: Hidden Monsters with SPHEREx I: A goldmine for heavily reddened quasars at cosmic noon
comment: Submitted to A&A 5th May 2026
summary: Heavily reddened quasars (HRQs) are luminous, dust-obscured broad-line quasars thought to represent a short-lived phase of intense black hole growth and feedback. Previous studies have been limited by small sample sizes, restricting robust statistical analysis. We expand the sample of the most luminous HRQs to enable population-level studies, connecting their spectral energy distributions (SEDs) to other quasar populations and placing them within an evolutionary sequence of massive galaxy and black hole formation. We assemble multiwavelength broadband photometry for the brightest HRQ candidates (K$_{AB}$ < 18 mag) and select AGN with red near-infrared colours (J-K)$_{AB}$ > 1.6. Using SPHEREx spectrophotometry, we confirm HRQs and determine redshifts. Detailed SED fitting allows comparison with other luminous quasars, including a control sample of hyper-luminous, unobscured Quaia quasars and luminous Hot Dust-Obscured Galaxies (Hot DOGs). We confirm 77 new HRQs with redshifts 1.5 < z < 3.9, dust-corrected optical continuum luminosities log$_{10}(λL_λ(3000A)$ [erg/s])>47.0, and line-of-sight extinctions 0.4 < E(B-V) < 1.6 (A$_V$ mag). This more than doubles the known HRQs at z > 1.5, including the first seven at z > 3. A UV excess consistent with scattered quasar emission is detected in 76% of HRQs. We show that HRQs are hot-dust poor compared to blue quasars of similar luminosity and redshift. Their 6um continuum luminosities are systematically fainter at fixed 3000A continuum luminosity relative to blue Quaia quasars, indicating deficiency in both hot and warm dust. These results support a scenario in which HRQs represent a blow-out phase, where strong feedback begins clearing obscuring material from central regions.

AI.tldr: This study expands the sample of heavily reddened quasars (HRQs) from 77 new sources (z=1.5-3.9), more than doubling known HRQs at z>1.5. Using SPHEREx spectrophotometry and multiwavelength SED fitting, they find HRQs are hot-dust poor compared to unobscured quasars, with 76% showing UV excess from scattered emission. These results support an evolutionary scenario where HRQs represent a blow-out phase with feedback clearing obscuring material.
AI.motivation: Heavily reddened quasars (HRQs) are thought to be a short-lived phase of intense black hole growth and feedback, but previous studies have been limited by small sample sizes, restricting robust statistical analysis. The authors aim to expand the sample of the most luminous HRQs to enable population-level studies and connect them to other quasar populations within an evolutionary sequence.
AI.method: The authors assembled multiwavelength broadband photometry for bright HRQ candidates (K_AB < 18 mag) with red near-infrared colors (J-K)_AB > 1.6. They used SPHEREx spectrophotometry to confirm HRQs and determine redshifts, followed by detailed SED fitting. A control sample of hyper-luminous unobscured Quaia quasars and Hot Dust-Obscured Galaxies (Hot DOGs) was used for comparison.
AI.result: 77 new HRQs confirmed at redshifts 1.5<z<3.9 with dust-corrected optical luminosities log(λL_λ(3000Å))>47.0 erg/s and extinctions 0.4<E(B-V)<1.6. This more than doubles known HRQs at z>1.5, including the first seven at z>3. A UV excess consistent with scattered quasar emission was detected in 76% of HRQs. HRQs are hot-dust poor compared to blue quasars of similar luminosity and redshift, with systematically fainter 6μm continuum luminosities.
AI.conclusion: The results support a scenario in which HRQs represent a blow-out phase, where strong feedback begins clearing obscuring material from central regions of massive galaxies and their black holes.

title: Magnetar field dynamics driven by chiral anomalies without magnetic helicity
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures. Submitted for publication. Comments are welcome
summary: The chiral magnetic effect (CME), arising from the chiral anomaly and enabling a mutual conversion between magnetic topology and fermionic chirality, is a key mechanism in magnetar field evolution. Previous work by Dehman & Pons (2025) demonstrated that the CME can efficiently generate dipolar fields ($B_{\rm dip} \gtrsim 10^{14}~\mathrm{G}$), consistent with magnetar timing measurements, provided that the initial magnetic field carries net helicity. However, whether neutron stars are born with magnetic helicity remains uncertain. In this work, we investigate the CME across a range of initial helicity configurations, including non-helical initial conditions. We find that the CME efficiently generates magnetar-strength dipoles on timescales of decades, independently of the initial helicity content. The instability is driven by localized helical structures that induce a residual chiral asymmetry and is primarily governed by the maximum chiral chemical potential, requiring $μ_5^{\rm max} \gtrsim \mathrm{few}\times10^{-11}~\mathrm{MeV}$ for onset in the magnetar regime. Our results further show that these dipoles may either remain stable and subsequently evolve through standard Ohmic decay, or become unstable if they acquire sufficient helicity, in which case they decay through the chiral anomaly, transferring energy to less helical modes. This outcome depends sensitively on the initial helicity distribution. These findings extend the applicability of the CME to more realistic magnetic-field configurations and underscore the importance of the helicity distribution at birth, a quantity that remains poorly constrained in neutron star formation, yet is crucial for determining neutron star magnetic evolution and magnetar formation.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that the chiral magnetic effect (CME) can generate magnetar-strength dipole fields (~10^14 G) within decades regardless of the initial magnetic helicity, requiring only a maximum chiral chemical potential ~10^-11 MeV. Dipole stability depends on helicity distribution: stable fields undergo Ohmic decay, while helicity-rich fields decay via chiral anomaly into less helical modes.
AI.motivation: Prior work (Dehman & Pons 2025) showed CME generates strong dipolar fields only if neutron stars are born with net magnetic helicity, but whether this occurs is uncertain. The authors aim to test CME under more realistic, non-helical initial conditions.
AI.method: The authors numerically investigate CME across a range of initial helicity configurations, including non-helical initial conditions, and analyze the role of localized helical structures and the maximum chiral chemical potential threshold.
AI.result: CME generates magnetar-strength dipoles (~10^14 G) on decade timescales independently of initial helicity content; requires μ5^max ≳ few×10^-11 MeV. Dipoles may remain stable (undergoing Ohmic decay) or become unstable (decaying via chiral anomaly into less helical modes), depending sensitively on the initial helicity distribution.
AI.conclusion: The CME applies to realistic magnetic configurations even without net initial helicity. The helicity distribution at birth is poorly constrained yet crucial for neutron star magnetic evolution and magnetar formation.

title: Spectrally and spatially resolved (sub)millimeter HCN-to-HCO$^{+}$ flux ratios in nearby ultraluminous infrared galaxies
comment: 24 pages, 9 figures. ApJ accepted
summary: We present the results of our investigations of spectrally and spatially resolved (sub)millimeter HCN-to-HCO$^{+}$ flux ratios at J=2-1, J=3-2, and/or J=4-3 in 18 nearby ($z <$ 0.15) ultraluminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs), using ALMA $\lesssim$0.2" ($\lesssim$500 pc) resolution data. The geometry of elevated HCN-to-HCO$^{+}$ flux ratios (with $>$3$σ$ detections for both molecular lines) in position-position-velocity (PPV) space is visually classified into (i) spherical shell (spectrally and spatially distinct), (ii) spectrally distinct and spatially compact, and (iii) filled (spectrally filled and spatially compact). These can naturally be explained by the elevation of the flux ratio due to (i) a spatially resolved outflow, (ii) an AGN and/or a spatially unresolved outflow with blueshifted and redshifted emission components, and (iii) an AGN and/or a spatially confined outflow with not clearly separated blueshifted and redshifted velocity components, respectively. Signatures of elevated HCN-to-HCO$^{+}$ flux ratios originated from (a) spatially resolved outflow and (b) AGN and/or spatially unresolved outflow are seen in seven and nine ULIRGs, respectively. In the former spatially resolved outflow-origin case, modest-velocity components relative to the maximum outflow velocity tend to be probed by spaxels with elevated HCN-to-HCO$^{+}$ flux ratios. The spectrally and spatially resolved HCN-to-HCO$^{+}$ flux ratios can provide additional information on the physical origin of the elevated flux ratios in nearby ULIRG nuclei, compared to previously conducted spatially integrated and/or velocity-integrated analyses.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes spatially and spectrally resolved HCN-to-HCO+ flux ratios in 18 nearby ULIRGs using ALMA data, classifying elevated ratios into three geometric types corresponding to outflows and/or AGN activity, with resolved outflows dominating in 7 cases and AGN/unresolved outflows in 9.
AI.motivation: To understand the physical origins of elevated HCN-to-HCO+ flux ratios in ULIRG nuclei, moving beyond spatially/velocity-integrated analyses by using high-resolution ALMA data to resolve the spatial and spectral structure of these ratios.
AI.method: ALMA observations at ≤0.2" (≤500 pc) resolution of HCN and HCO+ lines (J=2-1, 3-2, 4-3) in 18 ULIRGs at z<0.15. Elevated ratio regions were visually classified in PPV space into three geometric categories (spherical shell, spectrally distinct compact, filled), interpreted as outflow, AGN/unresolved outflow with blueshifted/redshifted components, and AGN/confined outflow, respectively.
AI.result: Seven ULIRGs show elevated ratios from spatially resolved outflows, nine from AGN and/or spatially unresolved outflows. In the resolved outflow case, modest-velocity components are preferentially associated with elevated ratios. Spatially/spectrally resolved analysis provides additional diagnostics beyond integrated approaches.
AI.conclusion: Spectrally and spatially resolved HCN-to-HCO+ flux ratios in ULIRGs can distinguish between outflow-dominated and AGN-dominated origins of the elevated ratios, providing a powerful diagnostic for the physical conditions in galaxy nuclei.

authors: Mithi A. C. de los Reyes
title: $V/σ$ Trends with Mass for Dwarf Galaxies from the Marvelous Massive Dwarfs Suite
comment: 26 pages, 12 figures, submitted to ApJ
summary: Galaxy formation scenarios can be interpreted through galaxy morphology and the level of rotational versus pressure support, quantified through the ratio of a galaxy's rotation speed to its velocity dispersion: $V/σ$. Observational studies of dwarf galaxies find that $V/σ$ does not strongly depend on environment, and may weakly depend on galaxy mass, which could shift our understanding of how dwarf galaxies form. We utilize the Marvelous Massive Dwarfs suite to examine whether $V/σ$ depends on mass in simulations, and understand how this varies for different baryonic components of the galaxy: HI gas, young stars ($<$ 1 Gyr) and old stars ($>$ 1 Gyr). We use a simulation sample of 67 isolated dwarf galaxies with M$_\star=10^6-10^9$ M$_\odot$ and produce line-of-sight maps for rotation speed and dispersion for different viewing angles of each galaxy. We find that $V/σ$ increases with mass, and that HI gas and young stars are more rotation-supported ($V/σ\approx 1-13$) while old stars are more dispersion-supported ($V/σ\approx 0.2-5$). This result is consistent with the scenario where young stars are born from dynamically cold gas in the interstellar medium and undergo dynamical heating over time. We quantify the effects of spatial resolution in observational determinations of $V/σ$ and find that existing observations using old stars may underestimate the intrinsic $V/σ$. We find a correlation between $V/σ_\mathrm{HI,global}$ and HI line profile shape that is qualitatively similar to previous simulation results, but we find higher $V/σ_\mathrm{HI,global}$ compared to prior work which found values $\lesssim 2$ for most galaxies in this mass range. Our results motivate future work to examine $V/σ$ and dwarf galaxy formation with different kinematic tracers of the galaxy.

AI.tldr: This study uses simulations of 67 isolated dwarf galaxies to show that V/σ (rotation-to-dispersion ratio) increases with mass, with HI gas and young stars being more rotation-supported (V/σ≈1-13) while old stars are more dispersion-supported (V/σ≈0.2-5). Observations using old stars may underestimate intrinsic V/σ, and the results support the scenario where young stars form from dynamically cold gas and undergo dynamical heating over time.
AI.motivation: To examine whether V/σ depends on mass in dwarf galaxy simulations and understand how this varies for different baryonic components (HI gas, young stars, old stars), as observational studies find V/σ does not strongly depend on environment and may weakly depend on mass, potentially shifting our understanding of dwarf galaxy formation.
AI.method: Utilized the Marvelous Massive Dwarfs suite with 67 simulated isolated dwarf galaxies (M⋆=10⁶-10⁹ M☉), produced line-of-sight maps for rotation speed and dispersion at different viewing angles, and quantified effects of spatial resolution on observational determinations of V/σ.
AI.result: V/σ increases with mass; HI gas and young stars are more rotation-supported (V/σ≈1-13) while old stars are more dispersion-supported (V/σ≈0.2-5). Existing observations using old stars may underestimate intrinsic V/σ. A correlation between V/σ_HI,global and HI line profile shape was found, with higher V/σ_HI,global than prior work (which found values ≲2).
AI.conclusion: Results are consistent with young stars forming from dynamically cold gas and undergoing dynamical heating over time. Future work should examine V/σ and dwarf galaxy formation with different kinematic tracers.

title: $Ab$ $initio$ modeling of Galactic dust polarized CMB foreground
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, contribution to the 2026 Cosmology session of the 60th Rencontres de Moriond
summary: We present the analysis of high-resolution synthetic dust polarization maps derived from large-scale simulations of magnetized multiphase interstellar turbulence carried out with the AthenaK code on the $Frontier$ exascale supercomputer at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Our turbulence model accurately captures spectral properties of the $E$- and $B$-modes measured by $Planck$ at 353 GHz. The simulations provide new insights into the physical origins of the observed $E/B$ asymmetry and positive $TE$ signal, facilitating the development of advanced models of Galactic foreground emission for current and future CMB experiments.

AI.tldr: High-resolution synthetic dust polarization maps from exascale simulations of magnetized interstellar turbulence reproduce Planck's E/B-mode spectra and provide insights into foreground emission for CMB experiments.
AI.motivation: To understand the physical origins of observed E/B asymmetry and positive TE signal in Galactic dust polarization, and to develop improved foreground models for CMB experiments.
AI.method: Large-scale simulations of magnetized multiphase interstellar turbulence using the AthenaK code on the Frontier exascale supercomputer, producing synthetic high-resolution dust polarization maps.
AI.result: The turbulence model accurately captures spectral properties of E- and B-modes measured by Planck at 353 GHz.
AI.conclusion: The simulations provide new physical insights into dust polarization foregrounds, facilitating advanced foreground modeling for current and future CMB experiments.

title: First Interstellar Detection of Methyl Carbamate: A New Observational Anchor for Glycine Chemistry
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables, accepted for publication in ApJL
summary: Glycine-the simplest amino acid-has remained undetected in the interstellar medium despite decades of sensitive searches, motivating alternative approaches to constrain its astrochemical origin. A promising strategy is to investigate the broader $\rm C_{2}H_{5}O_{2}N$ isomer family and identify detectable members that can serve as observational anchors for glycine-related chemistry. Herein, we report the first robust interstellar detection of methyl carbamate toward the hot molecular core G358.93-0.03 MM1 using ALMA 1 mm observations. Ten unblended rotational transitions are identified, yielding a column density of (4.21$\pm0.84)\times10^{15} \rm cm^{-2}$ and an excitation temperature of $204\pm10$ K. We also searched for other $\rm C_{2}H_{5}O_{2}N$ isomers with available rotational spectroscopic data, including glycine, but none were detected, allowing us to derive upper limits on their column densities. The resulting abundance pattern deviates significantly from the Minimum Energy Principle predictions, highlighting that the $\rm C_{2}H_{5}O_{2}N$ family is shaped primarily by kinetic chemical process rather than thermodynamic equilibrium. The observed methyl carbamate abundance is consistent with a grain-surface formation scenario involving radical-radical recombination ($\rm CH_{3}$O + $\rm NH_{2}$CO), further supported by its correlated abundances with its proposed precursors, methanol and formamide, across diverse astrophysical environments. This detection establishes methyl carbamate as a new observational anchor for glycine chemistry, providing critical constraints on the formation pathways of amino-acid-related molecules in star-forming regions.

AI.tldr: First robust interstellar detection of methyl carbamate (a C₂H₅O₂N isomer) toward hot molecular core G358.93-0.03 MM1 via ALMA, with non-detection of glycine; abundance patterns ruled by kinetics, not thermodynamics; grain-surface radical-radical formation scenario proposed.
AI.motivation: Glycine, the simplest amino acid, remains undetected in space despite decades of searches, motivating alternative approaches to constrain its astrochemical origin by studying the broader C₂H₅O₂N isomer family and identifying detectable members as observational anchors.
AI.method: ALMA 1 mm observations toward G358.93-0.03 MM1; identification of ten unblended rotational transitions of methyl carbamate; column density and excitation temperature derived via rotational diagram analysis; searched for other C₂H₅O₂N isomers using available spectroscopic data.
AI.result: Column density of methyl carbamate = (4.21±0.84)×10¹⁵ cm⁻², excitation temperature = 204±10 K; glycine and other isomers not detected (upper limits derived); abundance pattern deviates from Minimum Energy Principle predictions; methyl carbamate abundance correlates with methanol and formamide across environments.
AI.conclusion: The C₂H₅O₂N family is shaped primarily by kinetic chemical processes, not thermodynamic equilibrium. Methyl carbamate likely forms via grain-surface CH₃O + NH₂CO radical-radical recombination. This detection establishes methyl carbamate as a new observational anchor for glycine-related chemistry in star-forming regions.

title: Dynamical evolution of Milky Way globular clusters on the cosmological timescale II. Terzan 2, 4, and 5 mass loss and collision tracking
summary: We investigate the long-term dynamical evolution of Ter2, Ter4, and Ter5, focusing on their mutual interactions, mass-loss behaviour, and survivability in the dense Galactic centre environment. We performed a suite of high-resolution direct N-body simulations over 8 Gyr, modelling three individual clusters that we also modelled as combined systems. We compared reference runs of isolated clusters with simulations of the full three-cluster system to quantify possible differences in mass loss, potential energy, and orbital behaviour. Our simulations reveal multiple close encounters between the Terzan clusters. The most significant encounters occur between Ter2-Ter4 and Ter4-Ter5, with their tidal radii exceeding the minimum separation. A notable case is the pair Ter2-Ter4, which approaches within 10 pc at a relative velocity of ~320 km/s. We found that the mass-loss rate is higher for the low-mass Ter2 and Ter4 systems in the combined three-cluster simulations than in our similar isolated runs, highlighting the importance of mutual cluster interactions. The common run clearly demonstrates that mutual gravitational interactions between clusters drive significant triaxial deformations, especially for Ter2 and Ter5, which evolve from nearly spherical to distinctly prolate shapes. In contrast, the isolated runs show clusters that remained almost perfectly spherical, confirming that the observed shape changes are correlated with the mutual interactions. The survivability and dynamical evolution of Galactic centre globular clusters cannot be fully understood without accounting for collective interactions among all systems within a few kiloparsecs. Our results emphasise the necessity of complex multi-cluster modelling in realistic Galactic potentials to capture the long-term fate of surviving and dissolved clusters

AI.tldr: Using 8 Gyr N-body simulations, the authors show that mutual gravitational interactions among Terzan 2, 4, and 5 in the Galactic centre drive enhanced mass loss, triaxial shape deformations, and increased dissolution risk compared to isolated cluster models.
AI.motivation: To understand how mutual interactions among multiple globular clusters in the dense Galactic centre environment affect their long-term dynamical evolution, mass loss, and survivability, which cannot be captured by single-cluster studies.
AI.method: High-resolution direct N-body simulations over 8 Gyr, comparing isolated cluster runs with combined three-cluster (Ter2, Ter4, Ter5) systems in a realistic Galactic potential.
AI.result: Close encounters occur (e.g., Ter2-Ter4 approach within 10 pc at ~320 km/s). Mass-loss rates are higher for low-mass clusters in the combined runs. Ter2 and Ter5 evolve from spherical to prolate shapes due to mutual interactions, whereas isolated runs remain spherical.
AI.conclusion: Collective interactions among clusters within a few kiloparsecs are essential for accurately predicting globular cluster survivability and dynamical evolution in the Galactic centre.

title: The diverse morphologies and evolution of low-luminosity edge-brightened radio galaxies
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures, 8 tables. Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Fanaroff-Riley class I (FRI) radio galaxies show centre-brightened emission from disrupted lower power jets, while traditionally more luminous class II (FRIIs), are edge-brightened, with relativistic jets terminating in hotspots. Population studies of radio-loud AGN (RLAGN) with low frequency, deep, wide-field surveys have revealed FRII-like radio structures at lower luminosities. We present the first high-resolution morphological investigation of a representative LOFAR-selected sample of low-luminosity FRIIs, to determine whether this new population is physically distinct from traditional high-luminosity FRIIs. Using new $1.5$-GHz Jansky Very Large Array (VLA) observations for a sample of 19 low-luminosity FRIIs, from the LOFAR Two Metre Sky Survey Data Release 1 (LoTSS DR1), with luminosities up to three orders of magnitude lower than the typical FR break ($L_{150} = 10^{26}$ W Hz$^{-1}$). We examine the compact features and perform spectral index analysis to identify hotspots, cores and signatures of restarting or remnant activity. We find a higher prevalence of cores and a comparable number of hotspots in the low-luminosity FRII sample compared to a randomly-selected sample of luminous ($L_{150}>10^{26}$ W Hz$^{-1}$) FRIIs selected from the same parent LOFAR sample. Approximately 32 per cent of low-luminosity FRIIs show restarting or remnant behaviour, while $\sim 32$ per cent are active FRIIs with compact hotspots. Our results show that FRII source dynamics occur at low radio luminosities, but reinforce earlier conclusions that the population of low-luminosity edge-brightened RLAGN is highly diverse. Binary morphological classifications should be used cautiously as a first step towards more nuanced investigations of the complexity of jet life cycles and evolution.

AI.tldr: This study presents the first high-resolution morphological investigation of low-luminosity FRII radio galaxies using VLA and LOFAR data, finding that these sources show a high prevalence of cores and diverse behaviors (active, restarting, remnant), challenging binary FR classification and highlighting the complexity of jet life cycles at low luminosities.
AI.motivation: To determine whether low-luminosity FRIIs (recently discovered in deep low-frequency surveys) are physically distinct from traditional high-luminosity FRIIs, given that population studies have revealed FRII-like structures at much lower radio powers than the classical FR break luminosity.
AI.method: High-resolution 1.5-GHz VLA observations of 19 low-luminosity FRIIs (L_150 < 10^26 W Hz^-1, up to 3 dex below the FR break) selected from LoTSS DR1, with spectral index analysis to identify hotspots, cores, and signatures of restarting/remnant activity, compared to a luminous FRII control sample from the same parent survey.
AI.result: Low-luminosity FRIIs show a higher prevalence of cores and comparable hotspot occurrence relative to luminous FRIIs. ~32% exhibit restarting/remnant behavior, ~32% are active with compact hotspots. The population is highly diverse.
AI.conclusion: FRII source dynamics occur at low radio luminosities, but the low-luminosity edge-brightened RLAGN population is highly diverse; binary FR classification should be used cautiously and as a stepping stone to more nuanced investigations of jet life cycles and evolution.

title: Potamides: Mapping Dark Matter Halo Shapes from Stellar Stream Tracks in the Local Universe
comment: Submitted to ApJ
summary: Stellar streams trace the gravitational potential of their host galaxies and offer a direct probe of dark matter halo geometry. Cosmological simulations predict that halo shapes depend on both baryonic physics and the nature of dark matter, yet observational constraints on halo flattening and orientation remain limited, especially for individual galaxies. We present Potamides, which utilizes the curvature of extragalactic stellar streams to derive constraints on halo shapes. We apply Potamides to 15 stellar streams from the Stellar Stream Legacy Survey to infer the projected axis ratios and orientation of their host halos. We find that some streams in our sample exclude large regions of halo flattenings and halo orientations. Systems with edge-on wrapping loops or sharp turning points yield the strongest constraints, whereas great circle-like streams remain largely uninformative. All streams in our sample support a spherical halo for a given flattening direction. These results demonstrate that stream morphology can provide halo shape constraints for individual external galaxies. With upcoming surveys (such as Euclid, Rubin, Roman, and ARRAKIHS) expected to discover large numbers of stellar streams, this curvature-based technique will enable rapid statistical tests of dark matter and baryonic physics through the shapes and alignments of halos and disks across cosmic time.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Potamides, a curvature-based method to constrain dark matter halo shapes (flattening and orientation) using extragalactic stellar streams. Applied to 15 streams from the Stellar Stream Legacy Survey, it finds that streams with edge-on loops or sharp turns provide the strongest constraints, supporting spherical halos. Upcoming surveys will enable statistical tests of dark matter and baryonic physics.
AI.motivation: Cosmological simulations predict that halo shapes depend on baryonic physics and dark matter nature, yet observational constraints on halo flattening and orientation remain limited, especially for individual galaxies.
AI.method: Potamides uses the curvature of extragalactic stellar streams to constrain halo shapes, applied to 15 stellar streams from the Stellar Stream Legacy Survey to infer projected axis ratios and orientations of host halos.
AI.result: Some streams exclude large regions of halo flattenings and orientations. Edge-on wrapping loops or sharp turning points yield the strongest constraints; great circle-like streams are uninformative. All streams support a spherical halo for a given flattening direction.
AI.conclusion: Stream morphology can provide halo shape constraints for individual external galaxies. Upcoming surveys (Euclid, Rubin, Roman, ARRAKIHS) will enable rapid statistical tests of dark matter and baryonic physics through halo shapes and alignments.

title: Constraining the Galactic bar using the M92 stellar stream
comment: 24 pages, 17 figures. Submitted to MNRAS
summary: Stellar streams are excellent probes of the gravitational potential in which they evolve. In the Milky Way (MW), globular cluster (GC) streams are routinely used to infer properties about time-dependent perturbations of the underlying potential. This implies that streams with Galactocentric radii small enough to be perturbed by the MW bar should offer constraints on it, such as its pattern speed, which currently has a wide range of values reported in the literature and is important when studying stellar kinematics. The GC M92 has a small pericentre and should be affected by the bar. It has a diffuse stellar stream, but confirming stream members has previously been hindered by a lack of spectroscopic data. In this paper, we use Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) observations together with photometric and astrometric data to obtain spectroscopic members of the M92 stream for the first time. We identify a clear spatial distribution and gradients in distance moduli, proper motions, and radial velocities that confirm the stream's existence. We compare the observed stream to mock streams generated in different barred potentials and estimate the MW bar's pattern speed $Ω= 29.1^{+0.7}_{-0.4}$ km s$^{-1}$ kpc$^{-1}$ and $\dot Ω= 0.7^{+3.5}_{-2.3}$ km s$^{-1}$ kpc$^{-1}$ Gyr$^{-1}$. This is the first time a stellar stream is used to probabilistically infer these bar properties, and it opens up an exciting realm of inner Galactic potential characterisation using stellar streams.

AI.tldr: This paper uses DESI spectroscopic data, combined with photometric and astrometric data, to confirm spectroscopic members of the M92 stellar stream for the first time. By comparing the observed stream to mock streams in different barred potentials, the authors estimate the Milky Way bar's pattern speed Ω = 29.1^{+0.7}_{-0.4} km s^{-1} kpc^{-1} and its deceleration rate Ω̇ = 0.7^{+3.5}_{-2.3} km s^{-1} kpc^{-1} Gyr^{-1}.
AI.motivation: Stellar streams can probe gravitational potentials, and the M92 globular cluster stream has a small pericenter that should be affected by the Milky Way bar. However, confirming stream members was previously hampered by a lack of spectroscopic data, and the MW bar's pattern speed has a wide range of reported values that need better constraints.
AI.method: The authors use DESI spectroscopic observations combined with photometric and astrometric data to identify spectroscopic members of the M92 stream. They then compare the observed stream's spatial distribution, distance moduli gradients, proper motions, and radial velocities to mock streams generated in different barred potentials to probabilistically infer the bar's pattern speed and its time derivative.
AI.result: A clear spatial distribution and gradients in distance moduli, proper motions, and radial velocities confirm the M92 stream's existence. The bar pattern speed is constrained to Ω = 29.1^{+0.7}_{-0.4} km s^{-1} kpc^{-1} with Ω̇ = 0.7^{+3.5}_{-2.3} km s^{-1} kpc^{-1} Gyr^{-1}.
AI.conclusion: This is the first time a stellar stream has been used to probabilistically infer bar properties, opening up a new avenue for characterizing the inner Galactic potential using stellar streams.

title: The Spitzer Spectroscopic Data Fusion -- Merged Spectroscopic Redshift Catalogs in Spitzer Fields
comment: Accepted for publication by RNAAS on 8 May 2026
summary: I present the Spitzer Spectroscopic Data Fusion, a collection of merged spectroscopic redshift catalogs covering fourteen of the most widely studied extragalactic survey fields. Building on the Spitzer Data Fusion multi-wavelength photometric database, the collection merges several publicly available spectroscopic redshift catalogs within each field using a 1 arcsec matching radius, delivers a single best redshift per source together with provenance and overlap flags, and is available on Zenodo at https://zenodo.org/doi/10.5281/zenodo.6368347 The dataset is regularly updated as new spectroscopic surveys are published. It is intended as a community calibration resource for photometric redshift training, SED fitting, and multi-wavelength cross-identification studies.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the Spitzer Spectroscopic Data Fusion, a collection of merged spectroscopic redshift catalogs across 14 extragalactic survey fields, combining public redshift data with 1 arcsec matching, providing a best redshift per source with provenance flags, hosted on Zenodo, and regularly updated for use as a community calibration resource.
AI.motivation: To provide a unified, community calibration resource of spectroscopic redshifts across major extragalactic survey fields, supporting photometric redshift training, SED fitting, and multi-wavelength cross-identification.
AI.method: Merging multiple publicly available spectroscopic redshift catalogs per field using a 1 arcsec matching radius, building on the Spitzer Data Fusion multi-wavelength photometric database, and delivering a single best redshift per source with provenance and overlap flags.
AI.result: A regularly updated merged spectroscopic redshift catalog collection covering 14 widely studied extragalactic fields, publicly available on Zenodo.
AI.conclusion: The dataset serves as a dedicated calibration resource for the community, facilitating photometric redshift validation, SED modeling, and multi-wavelength studies.
